articles.body: When I want a karaoke track or a dry vocal from a finished mix, I go to Vocal Remover and upload the song there. The page splits the file into two pieces: the instrumental with the singing removed, and the vocal on its own. I have used both outputs. Sometimes I need a backing track so I can practice a part. Sometimes I want the isolated vocal to hear a harmony I keep missing. I get both files from the same upload, which is the part that made me stop juggling two different utilities. The separation runs on a Mel-Band RoFormer model. I am not going to pretend I follow every paper in that family, but I can hear the difference from the old "delete the center channel" trick.

articles.body: When a soft-edged transparent PNG gets squeezed into 64 colours, does turning dithering on fix the edge? On the feathered sample below it did not: the edge error stayed almost where it was and the file came out 3.5 times larger. Every number here is tagged measured , inference or not tested , so you can see which is which. The samples and the yardstick Three transparent PNGs, all generated by a script, all 800×800, all fictional. A feathered orange-to-purple circle (126,939 B, 230,502 semi-transparent pixels), a rounded card with a drop shadow (28,596 B) and a triangle logo with a 1 px anti-aliased edge (58,744 B). Generated art has a lot of flat colour, so it compresses more easily than a real design file. Read the percentages as relative.

Send Node's built-in fetch through a proxy: undici ProxyAgent, NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY, encoded auth, SOCKS5, rotation and the errors each mistake throws. TL;DR Pass a ProxyAgent as the dispatcher. fetch(url, { dispatcher: new ProxyAgent(" http://USERNAME:PASSWORD@HOST:PORT" ) }) routes HTTP and HTTPS through the proxy. Import fetch and ProxyAgent from the same undici package. Built-in fetch ignores HTTP_PROXY by default. Node reads the proxy variables only with NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 or --use-env-proxy, available from Node 24.0.0 and 22.21.0. The undici versions must match.

articles.title: sat-solver: a SAT solver from scratch in Rust, from DPLL to CDCL
articles.excerpt: Boolean satisfiability, SAT for short, asks a simple question: given a formula over true/false variables, is there an assignment that makes it true? It is the textbook NP-complete problem, which is us…
articles.body: Boolean satisfiability, SAT for short, asks a simple question: given a formula over true/false variables, is there an assignment that makes it true? It is the textbook NP-complete problem, which is usually where the lesson stops. In theory it is hard. In practice, modern SAT solvers handle very large formulas, and they sit under package dependency resolvers, hardware verification tools and planners. The gap between "exponential in theory" and "works in practice" is filled by a handful of specific ideas. I wanted to understand them, so I wrote sat-solver : a boolean satisfiability solver from scratch in Rust, in two steps. First the classic DPLL algorithm, then CDCL (conflict-driven clause learning) in the style of MiniSat.

articles.title: 8 Classic PlayStation Games That Are Barely Playable Today
articles.excerpt: From Tomb Raider to Silent Hill, eight classic PlayStation games whose tank controls, cameras, or lost code make them hard to play today
articles.body: If you’ve ever watched someone play an old PlayStation game and wondered why their character keeps spinning around in circles, congratulations, you’ve already met tank controls. If you’re unfamiliar, here’s your quick introduction: With tank controls, pressing up moves your character forward in whatever direction they’re facing, and pressing left or right only rotates them, so with the stick alone, you can’t sidestep or turn on a dime. That’s manageable in a hallway. It’s much less so when you’re sneaking past a guard, lining up a shot, or timing a leap across a pit, which is why the same scheme caused trouble in just about every genre during the PS1 era. These eight classic games are the hardest to go back to, whether the culprit is tank controls or something else entirely.

articles.title: Dropping missiles from orbit? 2 European companies sign agreement to study the idea
articles.excerpt: Atmos Space Cargo will fly its first Phoenix cargo-return capsule on SpaceX's Bandwagon 3 rideshare mission, which is scheduled to launch this spring.
articles.body: A pair of companies in Europe have signed an agreement to study the feasibility of developing weapons that can be dropped from orbit. Atmos, a space company known for its Phoenix reusable reentry vehicle , will work with MBDA, Europe's largest missile manufacturer, on the new project. "We are assessing how proven defense systems and new orbital technologies can be combined to strengthen Europe's conventional deterrence and enable future defense capabilities," Sebastian Klaus, the CEO of Atmos Space Cargo, said in a statement on Nov. 18. The system that the companies are investigating is called Precision Orbital Deep Strike, or PODS. The companies said that their initial scope will center on design and feasibility, as well as technology integration.
